documents.title: Syllabus Minimum Requirements Policy (Artificial Intelligence (AI) Usage section)
documents.summary: The Syllabus Minimum Requirements Policy lists what every OSU course syllabus must contain. Its AI section, added by Faculty Senate on 06/11/2026, makes an AI usage policy compulsory but leaves permit or prohibit to the instructor. The rest of the page (course content, Core Education, WIC, disability statements) is unrelated to AI.
documents.stance_why: The policy sets no AI rule itself. It requires every syllabus to carry an AI usage policy and says "Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor", so the decision is handed to instructors.

units.why: This is a syllabus requirement addressed to course syllabi: 'All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy'. It is a P09 type rule because it mandates an AI statement in every syllabus, binds instructors, and is a before-course design duty.
units.anchor: must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations for student use of artificial intelligence

units.why: The sentence 'Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor' says the permit or prohibit decision belongs to each instructor, which is P04 (let each instructor set the rule). It informs rather than commands.
units.anchor: Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.

documents.unit: Division of Academic Affairs (Senior Vice Provost)
documents.title: University Guidance on the Use of Generative AI in Teaching and Learning (memo to faculty)
documents.summary: A September 2025 memo from the Senior Vice Provost introducing university guidance on generative AI in teaching. It names shared commitments, strongly encourages instructors to adopt the guidance and a syllabus statement for fall 2025, announces that a statement will likely become a requirement, and lists workshops and consultations.
documents.stance_why: The memo only "strongly encourage[s]" instructors to follow the guidance and add a GenAI syllabus statement "tailoring it with details of the specific approach", and speaks of "faculty autonomy". It sets no ban or permission itself, so the decision stays with instructors.

units.why: The memo says the guidance reflects 'shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence', which states the principles behind the university framework. It is P56 because it is an institution-level preamble, and it informs rather than directs.
units.anchor: shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence
units.frag_end: security of individual and institutional data.

units.why: The guidance is meant to 'support faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom', i.e. instructors keep the decision about AI in their courses. P04 fits best because it places the choice with the instructor; the sentence informs.
units.anchor: support faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom
units.frag_end: security of individual and institutional data.

units.why: The memo says the guidance aims to 'protect the privacy and security of individual and institutional data', a privacy principle for AI use. P50 fits since it concerns data protection; it informs.
units.anchor: protect the privacy and security of individual and institutional data
units.frag_end: security of individual and institutional data.

units.why: Instructors are 'strongly encouraged to: Follow the guidance for instructors about GenAI in teaching and learning'. It recommends adopting the university guidance, so P56 (institution-wide framework) is nearest, with modality should.
units.anchor: Follow the guidance for instructors about GenAI in teaching and learning
units.fit_note: The unit recommends instructors adopt the guidance; the type covers the framework itself.

units.why: Instructors are strongly encouraged to 'Add the GenAI syllabus statement to their syllabi, tailoring it with details'. It asks for an AI statement in the syllabus, so P09, modality should because it is only encouraged for fall 2025.
units.anchor: Add the GenAI syllabus statement to their syllabi, tailoring it with details of the specific

units.why: The memo expects 'a GenAI statement will eventually become a syllabus requirement', a statement that the policy will change. P54 is nearest (policy is provisional), though the change is the planned hardening of an encouragement into a requirement.
units.anchor: expectation that a GenAI statement will eventually become a syllabus requirement
units.fit_note: Announces a specific planned change (statement becomes mandatory) rather than a general review commitment.

units.why: The memo offers a workshop, drop-in hours, resources and consultations to 'help tailoring your GenAI syllabus statement', which is faculty support in learning AI, P63.
units.anchor: Register for the upcoming workshop

documents.summary: The Center for Teaching and Learning guidance has three parts: rules for instructors (which AI platforms, instructor use of AI for materials, student activities and feedback), a syllabus statement template with five icon tiers, and advice for writing a course-specific statement. Instructors choose the tier; the document sets duties around approved tools, disclosure and data privacy.

It sets no single stance.

units.anchor: instructors and staff are encouraged

units.why: The definition of AI as 'a broad set of advanced digital technologies' sets what the guidance covers, so P61 (define AI and scope).
units.anchor: refers to a broad set of advanced digital technologies

units.why: The definition says GenAI 'includes both standalone offerings, such as ChatGPT, and offerings that are embedded in other software such as Microsoft 365's Copilot'. It defines scope, P61, and brings embedded AI within it.
units.anchor: includes both standalone offerings, such as ChatGPT, and offerings that are embedded in other software
units.fit_note: Also states that GenAI embedded in other software (Copilot) is in scope, which touches P07.

units.why: The page explains that approved tools ensure 'Integrated security measures, Standardized protocols, Enhanced data privacy'. This gives the reason for preferring vetted tools, P50, and informs.
units.anchor: Integrated security measures, Standardized protocols, Enhanced data privacy

documents.title: Generative AI Guidelines for Ecampus Course Development
documents.summary: Ecampus guidelines for faculty and staff who use generative AI to develop online courses. They require discussion of significant uses, limit staff to OSU-approved tools, require full faculty review and labeling of AI-generated content, and bar staff from producing critical course content wholly with AI. Student use is not addressed.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines say "Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development, while upholding the authenticity and quality of the student learning experience", then attach conditions (approved tools, review, labeling). AI is allowed with limits, so permit.

units.why: 'Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development' is a welcome with a quality condition, so P02 (encourage) addressed to staff and faculty.
units.anchor: Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development

units.why: Ecampus 'will adhere to OSU's Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning, along with the following Ecampus-specific guidelines', placing these guidelines under the university framework: P56.
units.anchor: Ecampus will adhere to OSU's Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning

units.why: Staff and faculty 'should carefully consider the use of generative AI' that significantly affects authorship, instructor presence or student interaction, for example creating chat bots or AI-assisted grading. A caution on instructor and staff AI use: P59.
units.anchor: should carefully consider the use of generative AI

units.why: 'Ecampus staff will discuss implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer in the desired use-case' is staff and faculty working through consequences before use: P63.
units.anchor: Ecampus staff will discuss implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer
units.fit_note: Staff consult faculty on implications of a use-case; the type covers support to faculty in learning AI.

units.why: Voice automation should 'being transparent when it's employed', a disclosure expectation for AI in course media: P47.
units.anchor: being transparent when it’s employed
units.fit_note: Transparency about AI voice automation in course media, not only disclosure to students of grading or feedback use.

units.why: 'Ecampus multimedia staff will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full' limits staff use of AI in their own work: P59.
units.anchor: will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full

units.why: 'Ecampus staff will use only OSU's approved Gen AI tools when working with faculty-created instructional materials; use of non-OSU approved AI tools requires instructor permission'. Vetted tools and data: P50.
units.anchor: will use only OSU’s approved Gen AI tools when working with faculty-created instructional materials

units.why: 'Any AI generated content used in a course will require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy': a review duty on AI-made materials, P48.
units.anchor: will require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy

units.why: 'Learning objects created with generative AI will be labeled clearly' is disclosure of AI-made course materials: P48.
units.anchor: Learning objects created with generative AI will be labeled clearly.

units.why: Courses that use AI substantially to create content 'will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum' discloses instructor AI use to students: P47.
units.anchor: will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum

units.why: Future scenarios 'should align with the seven principles outlined in our Ecampus AI ethics statement and may require department approval' refers to an ethics framework and approval: P56.
units.anchor: should align with the seven principles outlined in our Ecampus AI ethics statement

documents.unit: College of Engineering (Academic Integrity Resources for Faculty)
documents.title: AI Chatbot Policy Example
documents.summary: A sample course AI policy from the College of Engineering academic-integrity resources for faculty. It allows chatbots as a library-style resource for errors, algorithm verification, small code snippets and limited writing help, bans having AI write the whole submission, and justifies the limits by preparation for industry and the need for fundamentals.
documents.stance_why: The example opens "You ARE allowed to use ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI, or similar AI chatbots as you would a library resource" and lists conditions, ending with "You ARE NOT allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write your software for you". AI is allowed within limits, so permit.

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
documents.title: Guidance on Drafting AI Use Policies
documents.summary: A June 2026 EECS statement setting a common floor for AI use across courses. It covers faculty use (materials, grading), student use (default fallback, embedded IDE tools, disclosure, recordings), research work (theses, venues, confidentiality), syllabus statements, academic integrity and detection evidence, and appendices on use categories and research disclosure.
documents.stance_why: The document says it "provides the common floor and vocabulary" while "individual faculty will set course-specific rules", and Appendix A gives a spectrum of nine use categories that "Course policies will specify ... to each assignment". It has a fallback (grammar only when no policy is stated) but leaves per-course permission to instructors.

units.why: The introduction says the statement 'establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses' and 'provides the common floor and vocabulary' while faculty set course rules. A unit-level framework: P56.
units.anchor: establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses

units.why: 'Where those documents conflict with this one, OSU policy governs' ranks university policy above the EECS statement: P77 (comply with existing university policy).

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), graduate programs (ECE, CS, AI)
documents.title: EECS Graduate Handbook 2025-2026, Section 2.21 Guidelines for AI writing assistance and proper citation and attribution
documents.summary: Section 2.21 of the 2025-2026 EECS Graduate Handbook (ECE, CS, AI programs) on AI writing assistance, citation and attribution. It permits AI polishing of the student's own finished content, bans AI-created content or research, warns about plagiarism and self-plagiarism, and requires a similarity check (Draft Coach) on documents submitted to examination committees. The rest of the handbook is program requirements and was not coded.
documents.stance_why: Section 2.21 allows AI only for narrow polishing: "acceptable to use AI tools ... to polish and correct grammar of content already created", while "Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research". Permission is limited to a narrow listed use, so restrict.

units.why: 'It is acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance if a student uses them to polish and correct grammar of content already created' is a narrow prose permission: P18.
units.anchor: It is acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance

units.why: 'Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research' bans AI-produced submitted content: P19.
units.anchor: Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research.

units.why: 'The key issue is to ensure students are doing their own unique work and avoiding plagiarism issues': P29.
units.anchor: The key issue is to ensure students are doing their own unique work

units.why: 'Plagiarism is a serious offense with both short- and long-term consequences': P36 as a misconduct statement.
units.anchor: Plagiarism is a serious offense with both short- and long-term consequences.

units.why: AI tools 'may create content that is effectively copied from another author': AI output may reproduce others' text, P31.
units.anchor: they may create content that is effectively copied from another author
units.fit_note: Warns about unattributed copying in AI output rather than factual errors.

units.why: 'it is recommended that students use Draft Coach ... to check their work ... for similarity with other works': P40.
units.anchor: it is recommended that students use Draft Coach

units.why: 'when a student publishes with journals or conferences under a professional society ... the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents' (self-plagiarism): P52.
units.anchor: there is also such a thing as “self-plagiarism,” as strange as that sounds

units.why: 'It is the School's requirement that students perform due diligence ... for all documents submitted to their examination committees': P40, a required similarity check.
units.anchor: It is the School's requirement that students perform due diligence

units.why: 'If a student encounters any further questions ... they should check with their major advisor and/or with the AHGP': P10.
units.anchor: they should check with their major advisor and/or with the AHGP.

notes: Coder A. Course layer inaccessible (collect file). The EECS guidance is coded stance delegates because it lists use categories (Appendix A) and a CTL tier template, though it also states a fallback (grammar only when silent).
